items.followUp: State four main postulates of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Identifies that electrons occupy permitted orbits or energy levels around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Electrons move around the nucleus in certain permitted orbits, each with a fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award for stating that only specific orbits or energy levels are allowed.

rubric.why: States why electrons in permitted orbits do not spiral into the nucleus.
rubric.description: An electron does not radiate or lose energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award for explicitly stating that energy is not emitted in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: Describes how an electron changes between energy levels.
rubric.description: An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower-energy orbit.
rubric.how: Award for describing energy absorption or emission during an orbit transition.

rubric.why: Gives the relationship between the energy change and the radiation involved in a transition.
rubric.description: The energy change is related to the frequency of radiation by ΔE = hν.
rubric.how: Award for the correct equation or its equivalent verbal statement.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted orbits, each having a fixed energy.
An electron does not radiate or lose energy while it remains in a permitted orbit (stationary state).
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower-energy orbit.
The energy change is given by ΔE = hν, where h is Planck’s constant and ν is the frequency of radiation.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and explain its formation using sodium chloride as an example.

rubric.why: Defines coordinate covalent bonding and identifies the source of the shared pair.
rubric.description: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award one mark for a shared electron pair and one for stating that both electrons come from one atom.

rubric.why: Shows how the electron-pair donor and acceptor participate in the bond.
rubric.description: One atom donates a lone pair to an electron-deficient atom or ion.
rubric.how: Award for identifying donation of a lone pair to an acceptor.

rubric.why: Gives a correct example of coordinate bond formation.
rubric.description: Ammonia donates its lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺.
rubric.how: Award for the reactants and ammonium product, or an equivalent correct equation.

rubric.why: Provides a second correct example of coordinate bond formation.
rubric.description: Water donates a lone pair to H⁺ to form H₃O⁺: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺.
rubric.how: Award for the reactants and hydronium product, or an equivalent correct equation.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
The donating atom supplies a lone pair to an electron-deficient atom or ion (the acceptor).
In ammonium ion formation, NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
In hydronium ion formation, H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺; oxygen in H₂O donates its lone pair to H⁺.

items.followUp: Define boiling and state two factors that affect the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: Defines evaporation as a surface process occurring below the boiling point.
rubric.description: Evaporation is the escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid into vapour, and it can occur below the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for identifying surface molecules escaping into vapour; include that it occurs below boiling point for full credit.

rubric.why: States the effect of temperature on evaporation.
rubric.description: Increasing temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of effect.

rubric.why: States the effect of surface area on evaporation.
rubric.description: Increasing the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of effect.

rubric.why: States how air movement and humidity affect evaporation.
rubric.description: Higher wind speed increases evaporation, while higher humidity decreases it.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating the effect of wind speed and humidity.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid into vapour; it can occur at temperatures below the liquid’s boiling point.
Increasing the temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
Increasing the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
Increasing wind speed increases evaporation, while increasing humidity decreases it.

items.followUp: What is an unsaturated solution? How can it be converted into a saturated solution?

rubric.why: Defines saturation in relation to the maximum solute that dissolves at a specified temperature.
rubric.description: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
rubric.how: Award one mark for the maximum amount and one for specifying the temperature.

rubric.why: Describes making a solution supersaturated by dissolving more solute at a higher temperature.
rubric.description: Heat a saturated solution and dissolve additional solute in it.
rubric.how: Award for heating and dissolving additional solute.

rubric.why: Completes the preparation by cooling the solution without crystallisation.
rubric.description: Cool the solution slowly and without disturbance; it becomes supersaturated.
rubric.how: Award for slow, undisturbed cooling and identifying the resulting solution as supersaturated.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
Heat a saturated solution and dissolve additional solute in it.
Cool the solution slowly without disturbing it; the resulting solution is supersaturated.

items.followUp: State the modern definition of an isotope.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining nuclear property shared by atoms of an element.
rubric.description: Atoms of an element have the same number of protons in their nuclei (the same atomic number).
rubric.how: Award for stating same proton number or same atomic number.

rubric.why: Expresses the modern definition of an element in terms of its atoms.
rubric.description: An element is a pure substance made up of atoms having the same atomic number.
rubric.how: Award for identifying an element as a substance whose atoms have the same atomic number.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of atoms having the same atomic number.
Thus, all atoms of an element have the same number of protons in their nuclei.

rubric.why: Identifies the atomic mass quantity being compared.
rubric.description: Relative atomic mass is the average mass of an atom of an element.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the average mass of an atom of the element.

rubric.why: Gives the standard reference used in the definition.
rubric.description: It is compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.how: Award for the one-twelfth carbon-12 reference.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

items.followUp: Write two properties of proton particles.

rubric.why: States the neutron’s electrical property.
rubric.description: A neutron has no electrical charge.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a neutron is electrically neutral.

rubric.why: States the neutron’s approximate mass.
rubric.description: A neutron has a mass of approximately 1 amu (1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
rubric.how: Award for either accepted approximate mass.

modelAnswer: A neutron has no electrical charge.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu (1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of the oxide ion, O²⁻.

rubric.why: Uses chlorine’s atomic number and the additional electron to establish the ion’s electron count.
rubric.description: Chlorine has 17 electrons as a neutral atom; Cl⁻ has gained one electron, giving 18 electrons.
rubric.how: Award for identifying that Cl⁻ has 18 electrons.

rubric.why: Gives the correct shell or subshell electronic configuration of chloride ion.
rubric.description: The electronic configuration of Cl⁻ is 2, 8, 8 (or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶).
rubric.how: Award for either complete correct configuration.

modelAnswer: A chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gains one electron to form Cl⁻, so the ion has 18 electrons.
Electronic configuration of Cl⁻ = 2, 8, 8 (or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶).
